narrative:
The model predicts you have a 34% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your preparation.

The prediction is driven mainly by three key aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. While this might sound positive, students who ultimately pass almost always share this clean record; in your case the model sees it as insufficient to offset other risks. The second strongest influence is your strong desire to pursue higher education. Nearly every student who passes also wants to continue studying, so this actually pulls the prediction slightly toward passing rather than failing. The third important element is your father’s secondary education level. This is lower than the education levels more commonly seen among parents of students who succeed, and it contributes to pushing the outcome toward failure.

Taken together, the lack of any past failures was not enough to overcome the combined effect of your father’s education and other background factors, resulting in an overall prediction that you are at risk.

To improve, focus on the areas you can control right now. Increase your weekly study time beyond the two hours you currently spend, reduce your eight absences (which are more than double the average of students who pass), and make full use of the family support you already receive. These small, consistent changes can meaningfully raise your chances of passing.
